name: Pulmonary embolism (Wells)
seoDesc: Pulmonary embolism (Wells): work out your result from the score. A free health calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary:
The Pulmonary embolism (Wells) calculator takes the numbers you enter and reports the result immediately. It is free to use, needs no account, and shows the working rather than just the answer.

Think of it as a shortcut for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Pulmonary embolism (Wells) calculator work?
sections.html:
The Pulmonary embolism (Wells) calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationships described below and reports every result it can derive from them.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the please tick all that apply); then you type in the score.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
What you supply, field by field
FieldUnits and meaning
Please tick all that applya single on/off switch — tick it for “Clinical symptoms of DVT (objectively measured leg swelling and pain with palpation in the deep vein localization)”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
HRa single on/off switch — tick it for “Heart rate > 100 bpm”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
Historya single on/off switch — tick it for “History of objectively diagnosed episodes of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) or pulmonary embolism?”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
Hemoptysisa single on/off switch — tick it for “Hemoptysis (coughing up of blood)”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
Malignancya single on/off switch — tick it for “Malignancy (treated cancer or cancer treatment stopped in the last 6 months or palliative care due to cancer)”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
Probabilitya single on/off switch — tick it for “PE (pulmonary embolism) as likely as (or more likely than) an alternative diagnosis”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
Scorea plain number with no unit attached.

7 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Pulmonary embolism (Wells) calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Surgery=-please tick all that apply − HR − hemoptysis − history − malignancy − probability + score

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• The option the calculation settles on.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Pulmonary embolism (Wells) calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the score — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Pulmonary embolism (Wells) calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The 7 drop-downs on this page offer a fixed list of cases. A value that is not on the list cannot be entered, and the nearest option is not always a good substitute.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Pulmonary embolism (Wells) calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the score, which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (7 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Score = 0. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Pulmonary embolism (Wells) calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
